To highlight the essential role of each component in the MMM model, we simulated five scenarios, where Scenarios 1 and 2 were designed to study the influence of cell type mixtures on SVG identification, Scenario 3 was designed to study the spot and platform effects, Scenario 4 combined all the above settings to mimic the real ST data, and Scenario 5 was designed to study the method’s sensitivity to prior assumptions. Specifically, in Scenario 1, the proportions of cell types 1 and 2 were uniformly distributed across space ( Fig. 1 C  ). We found that the    P   -values of MMM and non-cell-type-specific methods were well calibrated in the null case ( Fig. 1 D  ), and all methods could successfully identify SVGs in the alternative case; however, non-cell-type-specific methods could not clarify which cell type the spatial variations belonged to ( Fig. 1 E  ). In Scenario 2, we varied the cell type composition spatially, with the proportion of cell type 1 increasing from left to right and cell type 2 in contrast ( Fig. 1 F  ). Due to the heterogeneity in gene expression profiles between the two cell types, non-cell-type-specific methods identified their respective marker genes as SVGs ( Fig. 1 H  ), while MMM controlled type I errors by accounting for the cell type composition ( Fig. 1 G  ). In Scenario 3, we kept the cell type composition randomly distributed, but varied the spot effects     α  i    ’s spatially ( Fig. 1 I  ) and added gene-specific platform effects     γ  g    ’s ( Fig. 1 J  ). This was designed to examine the robustness of the methods in the presence of batch effects and platform differences. Under the null condition, MMM still produced well-calibrated    P   -values for both cell types by explicitly correcting for these two effects, while Celina yielded slightly inflated results ( Fig. 1 K  ). Celina’s unsatisfactory control of type I errors in this scenario is likely due to its modeling of normalized data instead of raw count data. The data transformation step before analysis can lead to an inadequate characterization of the mean–variance relationship inherent in raw count data and introduce systematic errors ( 23 ,  39 ), thus preventing the full elimination of confounding bias. In Scenario 4, we combined the settings of Scenarios 2 and 3 so that the cell type composition varied spatially, as well as varying spot effects and gene-specific platform effects. We should note that Scenario 4 was the most challenging and also the closest to real ST data. We then set the false discovery rate cutoff at 0.05 and measured the power of MMM and other cell-type-specific methods in the alternative case ( Fig. 1 L  ). We found that MMM was more powerful than the other two methods across all settings of spatial pattern and sample size because of its ability to aggregate information from multiple kernels corresponding to diverse spatial patterns and correction for spot effects and platform effects. Compared to Celina, the power gain of MMM is due to its modeling of raw count data, which avoids the loss of information ( 23 ,  40 ). C-SIDE suffered from low statistical power since its nonparametric mode is not effective in combining the    P   -values corresponding to multiple basis functions (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). However, we should emphasize that its performance here does not reflect the effectiveness in the task for which it was originally designed. In Scenario 5, we generated data with varied prior distributions, including “flat top,” “skew,” and “bimodal” ( Fig. 1 M  ), to evaluate whether MMM is sensitive to prior assumptions (more prior settings in   SI Appendix , Fig. S1 ). We examined MMM under the null condition first ( Fig. 1 N  ) and then in the alternative case ( Fig. 1 O  ). The obtained    P   -values were well calibrated in all settings, showing that MMM is robust to prior assumptions. In summary, MMM outperformed all existing methods in various scenarios, both in terms of statistical power and type I error control.    MMM Distinguishes Cell-Type-Specific SVGs from Cell Type Marker Genes in the 10x Visium Human Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Dataset. MMM Produces Replicable Results Across Multiple Adult Mouse Brain Datasets and Reveals the Heritability Enrichment in Brain-Related Phenotypes.  In this section, we applied MMM to multiple adult mouse brain ST datasets, including two slices profiled by the 10x Visium platform ( 43 ) and a 3D model constructed using 35 slices profiled by Spatial Transcriptomics ( 44 ). By comparing the results from several datasets, we showed MMM’s robustness and consistency across different sources and perspectives. We further showed that the heritability of cell-type-specific SVGs was significantly enriched in certain brain-related traits and diseases. Throughout the study, we used STitch3D to perform cell type deconvolution with a mouse brain snRNA-seq dataset containing 59 cell types ( 27 ) as reference.  We first focused on the two Visium slices of the adult mouse brain across the antero-posterior (AP) axis ( 43 ), which have relatively well-defined morphological characteristics and thus allow a reasonable and distinct comparison ( Fig. 3 A  ). For example, the thalamus is a paired structure of gray matter situated near the brain center, and the hippocampus exhibits consistent thickness and comprises curve-shaped subregions, including three cornu ammonis (CA) areas and the dentate gyrus (DG). Compared to existing methods, the    P   -values obtained from MMM were more consistent between two slices ( Fig. 3 B   and   SI Appendix , Fig. S6 ). Then, we focused on four cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM, including Ext_Thal_1-specific SVGs  Pcp4  and  Nrxn3  ( Fig. 3 C  ), and Inh_1-specific SVGs  Calb1  and  Gnas  ( Fig. 3 E  ). We found that their expression variations revealed by MMM within respective cell types showed replicable spatial patterns between the two slices ( Fig. 3  D  and  F  ). Next, we applied MMM to a 3D model constructed from 35 coronal slices of a mouse brain hemisphere along the AP axis. The original dataset was generated by Spatial Transcriptomics technology ( 44 ). A significant challenge in analyzing the 3D model was the presence of batch effects across the numerous slices. However, the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM exhibited spatial patterns that closely aligned with previous findings ( Fig. 3  G  and  H  ). This suggests that MMM is effective in correcting batch effects across the slices. To further demonstrate the robustness of MMM, we evaluated its sensitivity to different deconvolution methods and rotation of spatial coordinates. First, by integrating MMM with estimated cell type proportions by RCTD and STitch3D, respectively, we found that it produced consistent results for most cell types (  SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). Then, we applied MMM to the two slices rotated by 45 degrees and compared the results before and after rotation, showing its rotational invariance (  SI Appendix , Fig. S8 ). Overall, the cell-type-specific SVG identification results from MMM were stable and reliable in practice.    Fig. 3. In many recent studies, the integration of the risk genetic variants identified by GWASs with other omics data provides valuable insights into mechanisms that underlie complex traits and diseases ( 16 ,  46 – 53 ). For example, the integration of GWAS and scRNA-seq data is a promising way to reveal functional programs and pathogenic processes at the single-cell resolution ( 49 – 52 ). However, the heterogeneity within the same cell type and lack of spatial location information severely limit accurate investigations of cellular origins in the tissue context. Although some methods attempt to utilize the ST data to tackle the above challenges ( 16 ), the common cell type mixtures confound the results and prevent finer resolution analyses. Here, we conducted an integrative analysis of the GWAS summary statistics data from European ancestry with the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM. Unlike the heritability enrichment analysis for highly expressed genes in certain tissues, our analysis provides a unique angle to characterize risk genes within a spatially variable and cell-type-specific context.  To do so, we aligned mouse genes with human genes, which is a commonly adopted strategy for studying human traits and diseases ( 16 ,  46 ,  50 ). Despite the biological differences between humans and mice, arguments in favor of using mouse RNA-seq data have been well discussed ( 50 ). First, gene expression profiles are highly conserved between humans and mice ( 54 ), which is supported by a series of large-scale projects ( 55 – 57 ). Second, high-quality RNA-seq data are more readily obtainable from mice than from humans. Third, the key findings from mouse data have been successfully replicated in human data in previous studies ( 50 ). After aligning mouse genes with human genes, we mapped these genes to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the human genome based on reference annotations ( 58 ), and generated a unique set of SNP annotations for each cell type. By treating a cell-type-specific SNP set as the annotation set, we evaluated whether the corresponding cell-type-specific genes can explain a higher proportion of heritability for a phenotype using the stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression (S-LDSC) ( 46 ,  59 ,  60 ). Here, we considered GWAS summary statistics data for 30 phenotypes (  SI Appendix , Table S1 ), which can be roughly grouped into two categories: brain-related, including intelligence (IQ), memory, reaction time (RT), verbal-numerical reasoning (VNR), Alzheimer’s disease (AD), epilepsy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), anorexia nervosa (AN), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), bipolar disorder (BD), cannabis use disorder (CUD), depression, insomnia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessive-compulsive symptoms (OCS), posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), schizophrenia (SCZ), and Tourette syndrome (TS); and non-brain-related, including coronary artery disease (CAD), high blood pressure (HBP), pulse rate (PR), free thyroxine (FT4), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), type 2 diabetes (T2D), body mass index (BMI), waist-hip ratio (WHR), bone mineral density (BMD), height, and osteoarthritis (OA).  Note that we have two groups of genes for heritability enrichment analysis: cell-type-specific highly expressed genes identified from scRNA-seq reference data and cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM in ST data (  SI Appendix , Table S3 ). To differentiate the contributions of two groups of genes, we first examined the heritability enrichment of genes that are highly expressed in each brain cell type. After mapping these brain-expressed genes to the human genome, we conducted S-LDSC using its baseline model, which includes 52 functional categories (such as genic regions, enhancer regions, and conserved regions) along with a category encompassing all SNPs. For each cell type, we incorporated the SNP annotation set derived from cell-type-specific highly expressed genes into the baseline model and estimated their heritability enrichment across the 30 phenotypes. We summarized the results of the enrichment analysis in   SI Appendix , Fig. S9  and observed significant enrichment of these highly expressed genes in most brain-related phenotypes. In contrast, no cell types in this mouse brain study exhibited statistically significant enrichment in non-brain-related traits or diseases, serving as a negative control. To characterize the contribution from cell-type-specific SVGs, we further added an SNP annotation set derived from the cell-type-specific SVGs to the baseline model of S-LDSC, conditional on the cell-type-specific highly expressed gene sets. The results of the heritability enrichment analysis are shown in  Fig. 3 I  . We found that the SVGs of certain neuronal subtypes were significantly enriched in cognitive traits, such as IQ and VNR, as well as in psychiatric disorders, including BD, depression, insomnia, OCD, and TS. This indicates that within these neuronal subtypes, only a subset of cells in specific regions drives the corresponding traits and diseases by regulating the expression of genetics-informed genes. For example,  Nrxn3  was an SVG within Ext_Thal_1 cells ( Fig. 3 D  ) while its human homolog  NRXN3  links synaptic cell adhesion to cognition and its disorders ( 61 – 63 ). Mutations in  NRXN3  may cause developmental delay, learning disability, movement disorder, and behavioral problems ( 64 ,  65 ). We further performed a gene analysis using MAGMA ( 66 ) with GWAS summary statistics data as input and found that  NRXN3  was significantly associated with IQ (adjusted    P   -value     1.284  ×   10   −  4      ). In summary, the cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM have great potential to elucidate the mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases in the spatial context through integrative analysis with GWAS hits.    MMM Yields Robust Results on the 10x Xenium Human Breast Cancer Dataset by Accounting for the Uncertainties in Cell Segmentation and Annotation.  To demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our method for high-resolution ST data, we applied MMM to a human breast cancer dataset ( 7 ) generated by 10x Xenium, a recently developed imaging-based ST technology that enables measurement of gene expression at the subcellular resolution. The reference data were generated using Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex applied to FFPE tissues (scFFPE-seq) in the same study ( 7 ).  Typically, analyzing the Xenium data at the single-cell level requires two preprocessing steps: cell segmentation ( 67 – 69 ) and cell type annotation ( 70 ,  71 ) ( Fig. 4 A  ), both of which introduce significant uncertainties in the subsequent investigations. For example, in the cell segmentation step, imperfect boundary division can lead to the inclusion of transcripts from surrounding cells into the target cell, thus causing cell mixtures. More importantly, these transcripts may not belong to the target cell type ( Fig. 4 B  ). Second, cell type annotation in a deterministic way can also bring uncertainty due to imperfect segmentation. To demonstrate this, we applied RCTD to estimate the probabilities of the most likely cell type of each cell segmented by UCS ( 69 ). Notably, many cells exhibit a probability of less than 0.75 for their most likely cell type ( Fig. 4 C  ). Ignoring these uncertainties can lead to inflated type I error rates when identifying cell-type-specific SVGs. Moreover, outcomes from different segmentation and annotation methods can vary a lot ( Fig. 4 D  ), posing a huge challenge for reproducibility. Within the MMM framework, we use the log-mixture structure to account for these uncertainties in the probabilistic view, producing consistent    P   -values when using segmented cells from different methods as input ( Fig. 4 E  , first row); in contrast, ignoring these uncertainties may lead to substantially less consistent results ( Fig. 4 E  , second row). We also visualized the expression levels of cell-type-specific SVGs identified by MMM ( Fig. 4 F  ), some of which exhibited distinct expression patterns across different spatial domains, suggesting that these spatial variations were driven by the activities of other cells in niches with high probability. For example, the expression levels of  CEACAM6  within DCIS 2 cells were significantly different between the area surrounded by invasive tumor cells and other areas ( Fig. 4 G  ). To further verify this conjecture, we performed spatial clustering to assign cells to clusters based on their niches using CellCharter ( 72 ) ( Fig. 4 H  ). We found that DCIS 2 cells distributed in different areas were assigned to different clusters (blue and pink), indicating the differences in their microenvironment structures. We then applied niche-DE ( 19 ) to perform the niche-differential expression analysis. We noted that the identified cell type DCIS 2-specific niche-associated genes, which were differentially expressed within DCIS 2 cells in the context of specific spatial niches, had a considerable degree of overlap with the SVG results from MMM (  SI Appendix , Fig. S10 ). For example,  CEACAM6  was a niche-associated gene of DCIS 2 cells regulated by the presence of invasive tumor cells with adjusted    P   -value     5.550  ×   10   −  3       reported by niche-DE, suggesting certain signaling molecule interactions. This was also validated by applying CellChat ( 73 ), whose results revealed that  CEACAM  signaling pathway was an important component of the cell–cell communication network in this breast cancer dataset (  SI Appendix , Fig. S10 ). Notably,  CEACAM6  is a cell surface receptor that can influence intracellular signaling events and plays an important role in tumorigenesis, invasion, and metastasis in vivo ( 74 – 77 ). It was also found that  CEACAM6  could potentially contribute to the regulation in the tumor-stroma boundary, which was correlated with the efficacy of immunotherapy ( 78 ). Further investigations, such as  CEACAM6 -targeted antibody–drug conjugate, has shown promising improvement in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma therapy ( 79 ). Finally, we used g:Profiler ( 80 ) to perform a functional enrichment analysis for the DCIS 2 cell-type-specific SVG set (  SI Appendix , Fig. S11 ) and found that it was enriched in gene ontology (GO) terms including anchoring junction (adjusted    P   -value     7.621  ×   10   −  6      ), apical junction complex (adjusted    P   -value     8.208  ×   10   −  6      ), cell–cell junction (adjusted    P   -value     2.957  ×   10   −  4      ), apoptotic process (adjusted    P   -value     8.942  ×   10   −  4      ), and cell adhesion (adjusted    P   -value     2.604  ×   10   −  3      ).    MMM Provides Consistent Results Across Multiple Colorectal Cancer Datasets from Different ST Technologies.  To evaluate whether MMM can obtain consistent results between ST data with varied resolutions, we applied MMM to the human colorectal cancer (CRC) datasets ( 8 ) generated by multiple ST technologies, including Visium, Visium HD, and Xenium. Throughout the study, we used the paired scRNA-seq dataset provided in the same study ( 8 ) as reference. We chose the CRC data for two reasons: First, the extreme sparsity and high noise level in the Visium HD data make the analysis particularly challenging, allowing us to highlight MMM’s advantage in statistical power; Second, the paired Visium and Xenium data could be used for verifying the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the absence of ground truth.  In the tumor boundary region, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often the most abundant stromal cell type, and macrophages are the most abundant immune cell type, both playing crucial roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment (TME). Therefore, we focused on CAFs and macrophages to make the comparison between MMM and existing methods. Since there was no ground truth on cell-type-specific SVGs, we first applied these methods to the Visium HD data and then used the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the paired Visium data for verification. In the comparison with Celina and C-SIDE, we found that MMM not only identified more cell-type-specific SVGs but also achieved greater consistency between the Visium HD and Visium data (  SI Appendix , Figs. S12 and S13 ). This showed that MMM enjoys higher statistical power when handling sparse and noisy data and thus could obtain more reliable results. We also visualized the spatial patterns of the identified SVGs for CAFs and macrophages using the datasets generated by Visium, Visium HD, and Xenium ( Fig. 5 A  ). We found that the spatial patterns revealed by MMM were highly consistent between different ST technologies. Specifically, MMM identified the colocalization of two subpopulations,  MMP11  +  CAFs and  SPP1  +  macrophages, around the tumor boundary region, providing insights into the tumor microenvironment. High-resolution data have unique advantages when analyzing rare cell types. For example, CD4 +  T cells and CD8 +  cytotoxic T cells are sparsely distributed across the tissue, resulting in very low cell type proportions in the most Visium spots (  SI Appendix , Fig. S14 ). This low abundance poses significant challenges for the cell-type-specific SVG analysis, as the target cell types can easily be confounded by other cell types in the spots. However, in high-resolution data, such as the Visium HD data, a considerable number of spots exhibit high proportions of these rare cell types, making it feasible to identify SVGs for them and obtain reliable results. Specifically, we applied MMM to the paired Visium HD and Xenium data with a focus on CD4 +  T cells and CD8 +  cytotoxic T cells ( Fig. 5 B  ). The spatial patterns of the identified cell-type-specific SVGs by MMM still showed high consistency between the two technologies. Moreover, we found that CD4 +  T cells exhibited higher expression of  KLRB1  and CD8 +  cytotoxic T cells exhibited higher expression of  GNLY  in the tumor boundary region compared to other areas. These findings enhanced our understanding of the immune microenvironment in CRC.    MMM Reveals 3D Spatial Patterns of the Cell-Type-Specific SVGs in the Drosophila Embryo Model Constructed from the Stereo-Seq Dataset.  In this section, we used MMM to analyze a 16 to 18 h  Drosophila  embryo dataset within certain spatial domains to present more distinct spatial patterns of the identified cell-type-specific SVGs in the organ context. The dataset comprises multiple Stereo-seq ST slices ( 81 ), where spatial bins were created by aggregating     20  ×  20     DNA nanoballs into 10 µm    ×    10 µm-sized bins as described in the original study. The reference data were built upon a three-level single-cell combinatorial-indexing RNA-sequencing (sci-RNA-seq3)  Drosophila  embryo atlas ( 82 ) that matches the same developmental stage as the ST data.  We began by applying STitch3D to estimate cell type proportions and reconstruct a 3D whole organism spatial atlas based on 13 ST slices. STitch3D successfully reconstructed the central nervous system (CNS) and salivary gland, which fully recapitulated the morphology and position of the corresponding organ structures ( Fig. 6  A  and  C  ). We then zoomed in on these two specific regions and applied MMM to reveal the spatial patterns of cell-type-specific SVGs in the organ context. Compared to other tasks in which MMM was examined, the detection of cell-type-specific SVGs for the  Drosophila  embryo faced additional challenges. First, the Stereo-seq dataset is highly sparse with more than 95% genes in most spatial bins having zero counts. Second, only a small subset of spots are available for analysis when we focus on a specific region. Both data sparsity and the limited sample size severely restrict statistical power. Moreover, batch differences among multiple ST slices largely confound the results and may cause false discoveries ( Fig. 6  B  and  D   and   SI Appendix , Fig. S15 ). Despite the difficulties, MMM successfully identified cell-type-specific SVGs and enjoyed high statistical power by directly working on raw count data rather than transformed data while simultaneously correcting for slice-specific effects (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). We further visualized the expression variations of the identified cell-type-specific SVGs and found that these genes varied significantly at different locations within certain organs ( Fig. 6  B  and  D  ), suggesting that they may correspond to different developmental states or functions. For example,  jim  is an important transcription factor in neuronal diversity ( 83 ) and elimination ( 84 ), and  fabp  overexpression enhances autophagy and suppresses amyloid- pathology, leading to potential therapeutic interventions for Alzheimer’s disease ( 85 ). We also used g:Profiler ( 80 ) to perform a functional enrichment analysis (  SI Appendix , Fig. S16 ). In the analysis of the CNS-specific SVGs, we noted that the GO terms related to CNS development were significantly enriched, such as neuron differentiation (adjusted    P   -value     2.050  ×   10   −  4      ) and generation (adjusted    P   -value     4.979  ×   10   −  4      ). Discussion  Characterizing spatial variations in gene expression with cell type specificity is an important but challenging task for investigating the landscape of complex biological systems in ST studies. In this paper, we have presented MMM, a unified statistical framework for identifying cell-type-specific SVGs in ST datasets. The success of MMM relies on its three carefully designed features. First, MMM uses a log-mixture structure to decompose the measured gene expression at each spot into a linear combination of fractions attributed to different cell types on the log scale, so that the cell-type-specific SVG identification results will not be dominated by the marker genes of certain cell types. Second, MMM explicitly corrects for platform differences between ST and scRNA-seq data, which are commonly found in real data. In contrast, overlooking this difference can lead to misidentification of spatial variations. Third, MMM can aggregate the information across multiple kernels corresponding to various spatial patterns. Therefore, the overall assessment output by MMM is effective in detecting unknown and potentially diverse spatial patterns in real ST data. Through comprehensive numerical experiments, we showed that MMM enjoys high statistical power while appropriately controlling type I error. We also used MMM to analyze eight publicly available ST datasets of different tissues generated from various platforms with a wide range of resolutions. The experimental results indicate that even for high-resolution ST data, considering cell type mixtures contributes to obtaining more stable, reliable, and replicable results. MMM is also easily applicable to 3D datasets, providing more biological insights from the 3D perspective.  MMM directly models the raw RNA counts to avoid information loss, resulting in an appreciable power gain ( 23 ,  40 ). In contrast, ignoring the count nature of ST data can lead to an inadequate characterization of the mean–variance relationship and introduce systematic errors ( 23 ,  39 ). Since the normal distribution cannot approximate the sparse data appropriately, such a power gain is apparent in data with low counts, especially for the recently developed high-resolution ST technologies like Stereo-seq and Visium HD. However, when handling data with high counts, the Gaussian approximation approach is attractive since a more computationally efficient algorithm can be derived.  Finally, we discuss the limitations and potential extensions of MMM. First, MMM requires annotated scRNA-seq data for reference-based deconvolution of cell types. The quality of scRNA-seq reference data and how well it matches the ST data have a notable influence on the deconvolution results and, subsequently, on the cell-type-specific SVG identification. Although single-cell atlases are increasingly available, they may contain missing cell types or substantial platform effects. More importantly, some ST tissues may lack the corresponding scRNA-seq reference data. Second, the cell types of interest may be present in extremely low quantities, which can make MMM unreliable for such rare cell types due to limited sample sizes and significant confounding effects from other cell types mixed together. These limitations may not be reflected in simulations because of the idealized settings of cell type composition but have essential impacts in practice as shown in our analysis of the Visium adult mouse brain dataset (  SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). Third, while our nonparametric statistical testing framework makes MMM powerful in characterizing general spatial gene expression patterns, their clear biological interpretations still rely on specific scientific questions and further investigations, as illustrated in our real data analyses. Compared to the methods that work on the predefined covariates, such as C-SIDE and niche-DE (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ), MMM is more suitable for preliminary exploration in cases where prior understanding of ST data is limited. Fourth, MMM was designed to capture spatially correlated cellular heterogeneity by considering each gene separately. However, combining all genes together could provide gene-set-level information. For example, representing the variations of spots across all genes through the low-rank approximation ( 86 – 89 ) generates interpretable factors that can provide deeper biological insights, such as the identification of metagenes, and gene–gene covariation and coregulation analysis.    Materials and Methods   The MMM Method.  Let     Y  =    Y   i  ,  g     ∈    N    I  ×  G       denote the observed gene expression count matrix with the spot index     i  ∈   1  ,  ⋯  ,  I      and the gene index     g  ∈   1  ,  ⋯  ,  G     . To account for cell type mixtures, we first need to determine the cell type proportions       β   i   =     β   i  ,  1    ,  ⋯  ,   β   i  ,  K      T    ∈    R   K      of each spot    i   , where    K    represents the total number of cell types. This can be estimated using deconvolution methods ( 26 ,  34 ) with the paired scRNA-seq data as reference. We further introduce two effects, denoted as      α   =    α  i    ∈    R   I      and      γ  g   ∈  R    , to account for spot-specific effects and gene-specific platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data. Specifically,     α     captures the variations in total transcript counts between spots while     γ  g     accounts for the expression differences of gene    g    between scRNA-seq and ST platforms. As we are interested in cell-type-specific spatial gene expression patterns, we next introduce the cell-type-specific gene expression profiles       η    i  ,  g    =     η   i  ,  1  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   η   i  ,  K  ,  g      T    ∈    R   K      for spot    i   . Then, we consider the following hierarchical probabilistic model ( 26 ,  90 ) for the observed RNA counts in ST data:   [1]         Y   i  ,  g    ∣   λ   i  ,  g        ∼   Poisson    N  i    λ   i  ,  g     ,          [2]        log    λ   i  ,  g         =   x  i   T      ξ   g   +  log     ∑   k  =  1   K     β   i  ,  k     η   i  ,  k  ,  g     +   α  i   +   γ  g   ,         where     N  i     is the total transcript count for spot    i   ,     λ   i  ,  g      represents the underlying expression level of gene    g    for spot    i   ,      x  i   =     x   i  ,  1    ,  ⋯  ,   x   i  ,  C      T    ∈    R   C      is the covariate vector, and       ξ   g   =     ξ   1  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   ξ   C  ,  g      T    ∈    R   C      is the vector of corresponding fixed effects shared by all spots. The log-mixture structure (Eq.   2  ) separates the contributions of different cell types by representing     λ   i  ,  g      as the weighted sum of    K    cell-type-specific gene expressions     η   i  ,  k  ,  g     ’s after adjusting for the multiplicative effects      x  i   T      ξ   g     ,     α  i    , and     γ  g    . To characterize cell-type-specific gene expression profiles, we decompose     η   i  ,  k  ,  g      into three components ( 15 ,  23 ) on its log scale as   [3]        log   η   i  ,  k  ,  g    =     log   η   0  ,  k  ,  g     ⏟    log mean expression    +     b   i  ,  k  ,  g    ⏟    spatial variation    +     ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g    ⏟    nonspatial variation    ,         where     log   η   0  ,  k  ,  g       is the logarithm of mean expression of cell type    k   , calculated from scRNA-seq data. The term     b   i  ,  k  ,  g      captures the cell-type-specific spatial correlation pattern among spots at different locations, and     ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g      represents nonspatial variation. Given the mixed-effects model (Eq.   3  ), we now focus on how to distinguish the spatial variation term from the nonspatial variation term. For gene    g   , we use a stationary Gaussian process to characterize the spatial variations from the same cell type    k    across all spots and an independent and identical Gaussian prior for all nonspatial variations ( 23 )   [4]           b   1  ,  k  ,  g    ,  ⋯  ,   b   I  ,  k  ,  g      T    ∼  N   0  ,   τ   k  ,  g    K   ,    ϵ   i  ,  k  ,  g    ∼  N   0  ,   τ   ϵ  ,  g     ,         where matrix     K  ∈    R    I  ×  I       is a prespecified kernel function of the spatial locations      ℓ   =      ℓ   1   ,  ⋯  ,    ℓ   I     T       with the     (  i  ,   i  ′   )    -th element being      K   i  ,   i  ′     =  K     ℓ   i   ,    ℓ    i  ′       ,     τ   k  ,  g      is the scaling factor of spatial variance component, and     τ   ϵ  ,  g      is the variance of nonspatial variance component. In contrast to existing methods, our formulation presents several unique advantages for characterizing spatial gene expression patterns in a cell-type-specific manner. First, we begin the model design with raw count data rather than transformed data to avoid information loss. Second, the log-mixture structure (Eq.   2  ) accounts for cell type composition while simultaneously correcting for the spot and platform effects between ST and scRNA-seq data. Third, the mixed-effects model (Eq.   3  ) enables a statistically rigorous way to examine the significance of spatial variations. Furthermore, our model can be extended to identify cell-type-specific SVGs in the multiple slices case and allow for batch effect correction by modeling the slice-specific effects (  SI Appendix ,  Methods  ). In summary, these features enable MMM to seamlessly integrate with the count-based deconvolution methods, establishing it as a unified framework for identifying cell-type-specific SVGs.  To determine whether gene    g    is an SVG of cell type    k   , we can formulate it as a statistical testing problem with the null hypothesis      H  0   :   τ   k  ,  g    =  0     against the alternative one      H  1   :   τ   k  ,  g    >  0    . To evaluate the significance of the spatial variance component of each cell type, we propose a powerful score testing framework while considering the cell type mixtures. Specifically, we first develop an approximate algorithm based on PQL ( 35 ,  36 ) to fit the null model efficiently. After the algorithm converges, we obtain the pseudo data vector       Y  ~   g   ∈    R   I      in the linear mixed-effects form with the marginal distribution       Y  ~   g   ∼  N   X    ξ   g   ,    Σ   g       under the null condition. Here,     X  =     x  1   ,  ⋯  ,   x  I     T    ∈    R    I  ×  C       is the covariate matrix of all spots,       Σ   g   =   W  g   −  1    +   ∑   k  =  1   K    M   k  ,  g      τ   ϵ  ,  g    I    M   k  ,  g    T       is the covariance matrix,      W  g   ∈    R    I  ×  I       is the diagonal weight matrix, and      M   k  ,  g    ∈    R    I  ×  I       is the membership matrix indicating the contribution of cell type    k    to each spot. Motivated by the marginal distribution of pseudo data, we construct a cell-type-specific test statistic in quadratic form ( 28 )   [5]         Q   k  ,  g    =   1  2      P  g     Y  ~   g     T      M   k  ,  g    K   M   k  ,  g    T       P  g     Y  ~   g    ,         which follows a mixture of     χ  1  2     distributions under the null hypothesis. Here,     P  g     is the symmetric projection matrix defined as      P  g   =    Σ   g   −  1    −    Σ   g   −  1    X     X   T      Σ   g   −  1    X    −  1     X   T      Σ   g   −  1      . Note that     M   k  ,  g      contains cell-type-specific information to help address the confounding issue due to the mixture of cell types. The power of the above hypothesis testing scheme is obviously determined by how well the kernel matrix    K    matches the true spatial variations exhibited by the gene of interest within a certain cell type. Hence, we use the Cauchy combination method ( 38 ) to aggregate information from multiple kernels capturing various spatial patterns and calculate a calibrated    P   -value as the overall assessment. The technical details are provided in   SI Appendix ,  Methods  .    Seamless Integration with Cell Type Deconvolution.  Through our numerical experiments, we found that the cell type proportions estimated by the deconvolution methods play an important role in the cell-type-specific SVG identification, and thus keeping the deconvolution and SVG models consistent in terms of the definition of cell type proportion is essential to controlling the false positive rates and yielding reliable and interpretable results. Within the MMM model, cell type proportion     β   i  ,  k      represents the ratio of the transcript count from cell type    k    to all transcripts at spot    i   . Here, we highlight its difference with another definition based on the number of cells rather than transcripts. Therefore, we chose RCTD ( 26 ) and STitch3D ( 34 ) to estimate the cell type proportions for MMM throughout the study. Specifically, we used RCTD for the single ST slice case and STitch3D for the multiple ST slices case. For a fair comparison in simulation studies, we used RCTD for C-SIDE ( 15 ) and CARD ( 33 ) for Celina ( 31 ) as suggested in their tutorial websites. The above deconvolution methods all require the ST data with paired scRNA-seq data as input.  MMM offers a seamless integration with the results from the deconvolution step. For example, the cell type proportion     β   i  ,  k     , spot-specific effect     α  i    , and gene-specific platform effect     γ  g     can be directly inherited from the cell type deconvolution step. After plugging in these estimates, no identifiable issue exists when fitting the MMM model. While the first two are necessary (    β   i  ,  k      and     α  i    ), users can choose not to provide the platform effect     γ  g    , and our software would estimate it automatically by adding a column of ones in the covariate matrix    X    and treating     γ  g     as an intercept term. Comparing to fixing     γ  g     the same as the deconvolution result, we observed better model fits by leaving it unconstrained in practice. The reason can be that the deconvolution model may not be exactly the same as the SVG model, and the latter fitted one should therefore be more appropriate. As a result, we allow     γ  g     to be a free parameter in our software.    Computational Efficiency.  We analyze the computational complexity of the MMM method to assess its scalability. Given the RNA count matrix     Y  ∈    N    I  ×  G       containing    I    sample spots and    G    genes, we focus on one gene at a time since all genes can be processed in parallel in our software implementation. To fit the null model, the MMM algorithm requires     O    I  2       computations. In the statistical testing step, we need     O    I  2       computations to evaluate the test statistics. Therefore, the overall computations are quadratic to the sample size    I    and linear to the number of genes    G   .  We implemented the MMM method in the open-source R package MCube, which employs a carefully designed parallel computing framework to achieve high scalability and efficient memory control with user-configurable parameters. Notably, users can flexibly specify the number of worker processes along with the number of threads on Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms per worker. This hierarchical control empowers the maximal utilization of available computational resources. In addition, to address memory constraints inherent in large-scale kernel matrix operations, we handle matrices that are too large to load in memory through memory-mapping to binary files on disk ( 91 ). This approach enables the kernel matrices that exceed physical memory limits while maintaining efficient data access.  We also conducted a runtime benchmark on simulated datasets (  SI Appendix , Fig. S2 ) and recorded the computation time for all the real data analyses (  SI Appendix , Table S7 ). evidence_text:
Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP): A computationally efficient method for dimensionality reduction of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides critical insights into the spatial organization of gene expression, enabling researchers to unravel the intricate relationship between cellular environments and biological function. Identifying spatial domains within tissues is key to understanding tissue architecture and mechanisms underlying development and disease progression. Here, we present Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP), a novel spatially-aware dimensionality reduction method for ST data. RASP is designed to be orders-of-magnitude faster than existing techniques, scale to datasets with 100,000+ locations, support flexible integration of non-transcriptomic covariates, and reconstruct de-noised, spatially-smoothed gene expression values. RASP itself is not a clustering or domain detection method; cell types and spatial regions are obtained by clustering the RASP PCs, and the effective cluster resolution depends on the K-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph and a smoothing parameter β. It employs a randomized two-stage PCA framework and configurable spatial smoothing. RASP was compared to BASS, GraphST, SEDR, SpatialPCA, STAGATE, and CellCharter using diverse ST datasets (10x Visium, Stereo-Seq, MERFISH, 10x Xenium) on human and mouse tissues. In these benchmarks, RASP delivers comparable or superior accuracy in tissue-domain detection while achieving substantial improvements in computational speed. Its efficiency not only reduces runtime and resource requirements but also makes it practical to explore a broad range of spatial-smoothing parameters in a high-throughput fashion. By enabling rapid re-analysis under different parameter settings, RASP empowers users to fine-tune the balance between resolution and noise suppression on large, high-resolution subcellular datasets-a critical capability when investigating complex tissue architecture. 1 Introduction  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) assays measure gene expression at thousands to hundreds-of-thousands of spatial locations within tissue sections, enabling researchers to characterize transcript abundance  in vivo  at resolutions ranging from small cell groups to subcellular structures [ 1 , 2 ]. ST technology facilitates exploration of gene expression’s spatial organization, providing insights into cellular microenvironments and functional states of individual cells [ 3 ]. Two primary types of ST technologies exist: high-throughput sequencing technologies (sST) and single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization or imaging-based technologies (iST) [ 4 , 5 ]. High-throughput sequencing technologies, such as 10x Genomics’ Visium, capture mRNA transcripts at multiple sites or spots on a slide. The original 10x Visium platform offers a resolution of 55 μm, with each spot containing between 1–10 cells [ 6 ]. Emerging technologies, such as Visium HD, promise higher resolution of 2 μm, approaching single-cell levels, while alternatives like Slide-seq V2 capture transcripts with a resolution of 10 μm, also nearing single-cell resolution [ 7 , 8 ]. iST technologies, which reach single cell resolution, include platforms such as MERFISH/MERSCOPE (Vizgen), seqFISH, osmFISH, COsMx, and 10x Xenium [ 9 – 13 ]. A notable advancement in recent years has been the introduction of iST platforms that support the use of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples, allowing for use of archival tissue banks, increasing the use of iST technologies [ 9 , 12 , 13 ]. Additionally, probe sets used in iST technologies have expanded, with systems like 10x Xenium developing probe sets with up to 5,000 individual probes [ 14 ], helping to bridge the trade-off between sequencing depth and resolution, allowing for more comprehensive profiling of gene expression. As costs decrease and technology advances, ST studies will transition from analyzing small sample sizes to extensive investigations [ 2 , 13 , 15 – 19 ], generating multi-slide, multi-timepoint ST datasets covering millions of cells across tissues [ 2 ]. Larger datasets necessitate development of novel computational tools that leverage both spatial and transcriptomic data efficiently.  ST’s rich data allows tissue investigation at multiple biological scales, and computational approaches must adapt. On a cellular level, cell type assignment facilitates spatial distribution visualization, enhancing understanding of cellular structure and function in native tissue [ 20 , 21 ]. At larger scales, identifying tissue domains aids comprehension of complex tissue microenvironments. Identifying cell types and spatial domains is achievable with recently developed computational tools. Popular single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) tools like Seurat and Scanpy perform principal component analysis (PCA) and clustering on gene expression data while disregarding spatial context [ 22 , 23 ]. However, methods like BASS and FICT now incorporate spatial context [ 24 , 25 ]. For spatial domain detection, methodologies like BASS, SEDR, GraphST, STAGATE, SpatialPCA, CellCharter, Banksy, NichePCA, and MENDER exist [ 24 , 26 – 33 ], utilizing different model architectures to embed spatial and gene expression data into low-dimensionality spaces for clustering and domain identification. ST data is often sparse, so de-noising and imputing poorly captured transcripts is a desirable feature, and many spatially-aware methods provide this functionality [ 34 – 37 ].  Yet, current methods have notable limitations. While effective on a single ST slice with few profiled locations, they are computationally intensive, exhibiting slow processing locally, particularly on iST datasets exceeding 100,000 cells. With iST dataset generation increasing, efficient, spatially-aware dimensionality reduction algorithms are necessary. Many existing methods are also inflexible and complex, hindering customization of spatial smoothing or integration of non-transcriptomic covariates, such as those derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images or protein abundance metrics. Addressing these limitations is crucial for deriving meaningful insights from large-scale ST datasets.  In this paper, we present Randomized Spatial PCA (RASP), a computational method for fast, scalable, and interpretable spatially aware dimensionality reduction. RASP produces spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) and optionally reconstructs de-noised, spatially smoothed gene expression values. Importantly, RASP is not a clustering or domain detection method; cell types and spatial domains are obtained by clustering the RASP PCs with standard algorithms (e.g., Leiden/Louvain or Gaussian mixtures). The effective resolution of the resulting clusters depends on the K-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph used to define spatial neighborhoods and a smoothing parameter  β  that controls the strength of spatial regularization. RASP employs randomized linear algebra for efficient dimensionality reduction of large datasets [ 38 ], supports integration of covariates such as cellular density or sequencing depth, and exposes the kNN and  β  parameters to enable user-controlled smoothing. Tested on six real-world and two simulated datasets (including 10x Genomics Visium/Visium HD and subcellular imaging technologies like Stereo-Seq, MERFISH, and 10x Xenium), pipelines that cluster RASP PCs exhibit tissue-domain concordance comparable to or better than existing methods, with competitive runtimes. This efficiency facilitates systematic exploration of kNN and  β  to balance resolution and noise suppression in large, high-resolution datasets.    2 Results   2.1 RASP overview  RASP performs dimensionality reduction and spatial smoothing on normalized ST data, with the option to incorporate location-specific covariates. The randomized two-stage PCA optimizes computational efficiency while enabling the flexible and efficient analysis of high-resolution ST datasets. RASP utilizes a sparse matrix representation of the data, conducts dimensionality reduction via randomized PCA, and generates spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) using an inverse distance matrix sparsified by a kNN threshold ( Fig 1A ). Covariates integration into the latent variables is achieved through an optional second-stage randomized PCA on a matrix with covariates appended to first-stage smoothed PCs. RASP’s spatially smoothed PCs are useful for a variety of downstream analyses, including clustering and reduced rank reconstruction of gene-level expression. See Algorithm 1 and  Sect 4.1  for details. Note that by default, RASP utilizes 20 PCs, although this is a user tunable parameter. See Figs O and P in  S1 Text  for effects of variable PC number on RASP performance.   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.g001  Fig 1   RASP overview.   A: Method workflow.  RASP takes as input a cell-by-gene expression matrix and spatial coordinates from a ST experiment. The expression matrix is reduced via randomized PCA and spatially smoothed by a sparse inverse distance matrix. Non-transcriptomic covariates can be added at this stage (not pictured). The output of RASP can be used for downsteam analyses including cell type annotation and spatial domain identification.  B: Evaluation pipeline.  RASP was tested on four ST datasets each generated using a different platform (MERFISH, Stereo-seq, Xenium, Visium) and two synthetic datasets (100 replicates each). RASP results were compared against standard PCA and alternative spatially aware dimensionality reduction models (SEDR, GraphST, SpatialPCA, BASS, STAGATE, CellCharter, nichePCA, and MENDER) for both accuracy and speed.                        2.2 RASP evaluation on real data  We applied RASP to six publicly available ST datasets generated using diverse techniques and resolutions on human and mouse tissues including the mouse ovary (Vizgen MERFISH technology), mouse olfactory bulb (STOmics Stereo-seq technology), human breast cancer tumor (10x Genomics, Xenium technology), human DLPFC (10x Genomics, Visium technology), and Sagittal mouse brain (Allen institute, Vizgen MERFISH technology), and Coronal mouse brain (10x Genomics, Visium HD technology) ( Fig 1B ) and Table A in  S1 Text . For details regarding field standard preprocessing steps used, such as filtering criteria and normalization, please refer to  Sects 4.4.1 – 4.4.3 , and Sect 1.2 in  S1 Text , Sect 1.3 in  S1 Text .  We evaluated RASP by clustering locations using the spatially smoothed principal components (PCs) output by the algorithm. Cluster quality was assessed through spatial continuity and compactness via CHAOS score (Sect 1.3 in  S1 Text ), spatial autocorrelation by Moran’s I (Sect 1.4 in  S1 Text ) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) (Sect 1.2 in  S1 Text ) compared to ground truth annotations. We conducted a sensitivity analysis on key RASP parameters, focusing on the kNN distance threshold for sparse matrix construction and the  β  power parameter (see  Fig 1A ). This analysis used a one-parameter-at-a-time strategy to investigate parameter impacts on clustering outcomes.  Performance comparisons were made between RASP and eight other spatially informed dimensionality reduction or spatial domain detection methods: GraphST [ 26 ], SEDR [ 27 ], SpatialPCA [ 28 ], STAGATE [ 29 ], CellCharter [ 30 ], nichePCA [ 32 ],MENDER [ 33 ], and the joint cell type and domain inference tool BASS [ 24 ], as well as performing randomized PCA. For each comparison, we adhered to the respective GitHub tutorials to run these methods for spatial domain and cell type detection. Clustering of latent dimensions found by each method was performed using Mclust [ 39 ], Louvain [ 40 ], Leiden [ 41 ], and Walktrap [ 42 ] algorithms, where appropriate. For datasets with ground truth annotations, the ARI values presented are based on a default range of parameters outlined in  Table 1 .   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.t001  Table 1   RASP parameter suggestions. Obtained from Huang et al., [ 15 ] it includes ground truth cell type annotations based on histology and differential gene expression ( Fig 2A ). Annotations include luteal, luteinizing mural, granulosa, theca, and stromal cells, with clear spatial organization, alongside endothelial, epithelial, and immune cells, which are heterogeneously distributed across the tissue [ 43 ], making automatic annotation challenging.   10.1371/journal.pcbi.1013759.g002  Fig 2   Overview of mouse ovary analysis using Vizgen MERFISH data. White lines depict luteinizing mural and luteal cell compartment boundaries.                      For this dataset, RASP was set at the recommended ‘cell type’ default parameters ( Table 1 ), using Louvain clustering achieved the highest ARI of 0.69, followed by standard randomized PCA (ARI of 0.58) and SEDR (ARI of 0.57) (see  Fig 2A  and  2C ). We employed three different clustering methods to assign labels to cells in the dataset. The Louvain and Leiden algorithms performed best, while Mclust the worst. Note that BASS utilizes Mclust as a prior in its Bayesian framework but does not support a user-defined clustering algorithm.  Relative runtimes show RASP is comparable to nichePCA and one to three orders-of-magnitude faster than other methods on this dataset ( Fig 2B ). RASP performance diminishes with increasing kNN thresholds for PC smoothing; highlighted by decreasing ARI scores at larger kNN values ( Fig 2D ). This result is not unexpected for cell type annotation, but it is noteworthy that the local smoothing employed by RASP in this task, essentially borrowing information from just a few neighboring cells, has a marked increase in performance over normal randomized PCA for clustering-based label assignment.  Using RASP-based reduced rank reconstruction of gene expression profiles, we analyzed the spatial signature of the luteinizing hormone/chorionic gonadotropin receptor (Lhcgr) given its essential role in ovarian biology and ovulation ( Fig 2E ). Lhcgr is a G-protein coupled receptor that binds luteinizing hormone and chorionic gonadotropins, is expressed on luteal and luteinizing mural cells [ 44 – 46 ]. Originally, gene expression showed minimal spatial patterning ( Fig 2E , left plot). After PCA-based reduced rank and RASP-based reconstruction, expression is localized to luteinizing mural and luteal cells ( Fig 2E , middle and right plots). When comparing normalized expression log-2 fold-change (log2FC) between luteinizing mural and luteal cells vs all other cells, both PCA-based and RASP-based reduced rank reconstruction results in higher mean expression (localization) to these regions. For this example, we utilized the distances to only 2 kNN, which results in very similar log2FC values between normal PCA-based and RASP-based reconstruction.    2.4 Incorporation of covariates improves RASP annotation of mouse ovary ST data  A key feature of RASP is support for integrating non-transcriptomic covariates into reduced dimensions. The two-stage PCA approach used by RASP offers benefits relative to a single PCA on merged transcriptomic and non-transcriptomic variables: It prevents covariate signal dilution within the high-dimensional transcriptomic data, and decouples spatial smoothing of expression data from covariates. Library size and cell volume covariates where smoothed by the same inverse distance weighting as the PCs matrix, prior the second round of dimensionality reduction. In addition, we explored the addition of local cell density for the breast cancer dataset, using the same experimental design described above, with the RASP kNN held constant at 60. By enabling rapid parameter exploration and robust clustering on the entire Xenium dataset—without the need for sketching or specialized hardware—RASP empowers researchers to retain biological complexity and make high-confidence discoveries in challenging clinical specimens.    2.9 RASP can efficiently analyze Visium HD without the need for downsampling  We applied RASP to the publicly available 10x Visium HD mouse coronal brain dataset, which was aggregated to 8 μm spots, encompassing over 393,000 spots (393,543) and profiling 19,059 genes. We observed that the performance trends and parameter sensitivities for Visium HD closely mirror those from the mouse olfactory bulb Stereo-seq dataset (see  Sect 2.7 ), indicating consistent behavior of RASP across different spatial transcriptomics platforms and tissue types. Due to the computational burden associated with Visium HD’s large dataset, RASP was run on the full dataset without downsampling. In contrast, the other benchmark methods were applied to a downsampled version of the data, reduced to 10% of the original spots, to allow feasible runtimes while maintaining comparative context. These results are detailed in Figs X-Y in  S1 Text , showcasing the comparative performance and parameter exploration across all methods.    2.10 Simulation analysis  In addition to evaluating RASP on real data, we applied RASP and comparison techniques to simulated ST datasets generated using the  R  package  SRTsim  [ 59 ] for two different tissue models with 100 replicates each. The first model, the  Stripes  model, represents a simple tissue with a laminar structure of eight tissue domains (see Fig I in  S1 Text ). The second model, the  Dots  model, represents a complex tissue with heterogeneous circular regions scattered across the tissue, and a background cell type (Fig L in  S1 Text ).  RASP outperformed all other methods in computational speed and achieved comparable using default parameters. For the  Stripes  model, the ‘spatial domain’ parameter settings (kNN 30–100) is needed to correctly identify the laminar tissue-spanning domains (Fig I in  S1 Text ). For clustering  Stripes  data, Leiden and Louvain were found to be optimal, followed by Walktrap and Mclust. Similar to the olfactory bulb and breast cancer datasets, smaller  β  values (0–0.5) produced better results, with ARI values dropping for all clustering algorithms and kNN thresholds at higher  β  values (Fig I in  S1 Text ).  For the  Dots  model, the ‘cell type’ parameter setting (kNN 2–20) is needed to identify the regions in this dataset (Fig L in  S1 Text ). For clustering  Dots  data, Walktrap was optimal, followed by Mclust, Leiden and Louvain. Similar to the Ovary dataset, larger  β  values between 1.5–2.0 were found to produce better results, with ARI values dropping considerably for all clustering algorithms at lower  β  values (Fig L in  S1 Text ). Similar to the  Stripes  model, RASP outperformed all other methods in speed and produced accurate label predictions across its default parameters.    2.11 RASP facilitates scalable, multi-resolution exploration through computational efficiency  A unique advantage of RASP is its computational efficiency, which enables the biologically meaningful exploration of ST data at multiple scales. Across a diverse collection of ST datasets, spanning multiple tissues and profiling technologies, RASP consistently outperformed or matched other state-of-the-art methods while being orders-of-magnitude faster. In the complex, cellular-resolution MERFISH ovary dataset, RASP was one-to-three orders-of-magnitude faster than competing algorithms ( Fig 2B ). This speedup persisted even when annotations were spatially heterogeneous and challenging to resolve, such as immune and endothelial populations. SEDR was approximately one order-of-magnitude slower, and BASS nearly four orders-of-magnitude slower, highlighting the impact of algorithmic efficiency when analyzing large, high-resolution ST data. For datasets at anatomical or intermediate scale (e.g, the DLPFC, mouse olfactory bulb, breast cancer, and mouse brain datasets), RASP’s efficiency enabled practical multi-scale analysis that would otherwise be prohibitive due to memory and runtime constraints. Notably, in the breast cancer dataset containing over half a million cells, RASP readily analyzed the full dataset, a task that caused other methods to fail due to memory limits (requiring over 1 TB of RAM to train the model).  The computational speed of RASP allows users to systematically and interactively explore the effects of the kNN threshold and  β  exponent, supporting robust identification of optimal domain solutions tailored to the driving biological questions that motivated the experiment. For instance, in the ovary dataset, local smoothing (small kNN) and larger  β  yielded superior performance for cell type annotation, while higher kNN was necessary to delineate tissue-scale domains in breast cancer. Because RASP’s runtime is so low relative to alternative techniques, researchers are not forced to compromise on parameter search or multi-scale analysis, but can instead comprehensively interrogate tissue structure at all relevant spatial scales. Importantly, the rPCA embedding need only be computed once: subsequent parameter sweeps simply rebuild the sparse distance matrix, apply the inverse-distance weighting to the fixed rPCA coordinates, and rerun clustering. To guide choice of optimal settings in a label-free manner, users can compute spatial-autocorrelation statistics (e.g. Moran’s I) or boundary-coherence measures like the CHAOS score for each domain solution, and then select the (kNN,  β ) combination that maximizes these metrics. This workflow makes it trivial to identify biologically meaningful multi-resolution domains without ever repeating the costly dimension-reduction step. In sum, RASP’s computational efficiency not only matches or exceeds state-of-the-art clustering accuracy, but also fundamentally enables the multi-resolution, exploratory analyses needed to reveal the full complexity of spatial tissue architectures.    2.12 PC number impacts RASP performance  For the real ST analyses detailed in  Sects 2.3 – 2.8 , we computed 20 spatially-smoothed PCs using RASP and performed location-based clustering on the components. Determining the optimal rank for dimensionality reduction is a long-standing problem in statistical analysis and ongoing topic of debate within the bioinformatics community for scRNA-seq and ST data. In practice, analyses typically use a default of between 20 and 50 PCs. Tools like  Scanpy  and  Seurat  default to retaining 30 and 50 PCs respectively, serving as a useful benchmarks.  To evaluate robustness, we ran RASP using the best-performing parameters across the DLPFC, mouse ovary, and breast cancer datasets while retaining 100 PCs. We iteratively clustered each dataset using an increase number of retained PCs, from 5–60, to understand the correlation between PC count and cluster label accuracy (Fig O in  S1 Text ). For the DLPFC dataset, stable ARI values were observed with increasing PC number for the Louvain, Leiden, and Mclust clustering methods, and an increase for Walktrap. This invariance suggests these clustering models describe data distribution well regardless of dimensions. Conversely, in the mouse ovary dataset, we noted an upward ARI trend with more PCs for the Louvain and Leiden clustering methods. This behavior is consistent with the ground truth annotations of cell types present in this tissue, as higher order PCs are adept at capturing the nuanced details required for accurate cell typing (Fig P in  S1 Text ). Interestingly, Mclust improved at the lowest PC count, likely because Mclust assumes clusters have consistent size and shape, which isn’t the case here. In the breast cancer dataset, Louvain and Leiden algorithms showed increased ARIs up to 30 PCs, and then values decreased, while Mclust ARIs decreased as the number of PCs increased. This reduction in classification accuracy aligns with the nature of the classification task in this dataset, which deals with more extensive spatial domains rather than finer cellular granularity, thereby indicating that broader spatial domains might be more appropriately captured with fewer PCs (Fig P in  S1 Text ).    2.13 Influence of  β  on inverse distance weighting  To examine the effects of varying the parameter  β  on inverse distance weighting, we computed a sparse distance matrix representing the spatial relationships among data points. Subsequently, we applied an inverse weighting transformation to this distance matrix, raising it to different powers of  β . The relationship between distance (um) and the corresponding weights, calculated at  β  values between 0 and 2, is visualized (Figs Q and R in  S1 Text ). A  β  value of 0 results in a relatively uniform weighting across distances, effectively creating a rectangular kernel. In contrast,                 β  =  2      increases the importance of small distances, and down weighing the importance of larger distances. The inverse distance weightings for                 β  =  0  ,  1  ,  2      were applied to the first six PCs computed on the Mouse Ovary dataset and visualized spatially (Fig Q in  S1 Text ). Setting                 β  =  0      results in large-scale smoothing across the structures present within the tissue. In contrast,                 β  =  2      facilitates a localized smoothing effect, resulting in finer granularity of the observed structures. These results underscore the importance of  β  in modulating the influence of neighboring points on the distance-weighted computations.    2.14 Differential distance metrics and weighting analysis  For the RASP results presented in  Sects 2.3 – 2.8 , spatial smoothing was performed using a sparse inverse distance matrix where each element is computed as the inverse Euclidean distance (raised to the power of  β ) between ST locations, with diagonal elements set to either the minimum distance (or half the minimum distance for Visium technology). We choose Euclidean distance for a number of reasons. First, the raw spatial coordinates generated by any imaging-based ST platform (Visium, Xenium, MERFISH, Stereo-Seq, etc.) are expressed in real-space units (microns), and Euclidean distance is the natural metric by which physical proximity on a 2D tissue section is measured. Second, Euclidean geometry is both isotropic and translation-invariant: cells or spots that are offset by the same vector are treated identically regardless of orientation, ensuring unbiased smoothing across the tissue. Third, from a computational standpoint Euclidean distances can be computed efficiently and are straightforward to threshold or sparsify—critical for scaling to high-resolution, subcellular datasets. The inverse distance weighting of the Euclidean distance captures the biologically plausible principle that the strength of spatial relationships decays continuously with physical separation, with the  β  parameter allowing flexible modeling of interaction ranges, from highly local (large  β ) to more diffuse (small  β ).  To systematically evaluate the impact of both the distance metric and the weighting kernel, we evaluated Euclidean, Manhattan, and Chebychev distances as well as kernel-based weightings (Gaussian, quadratic), in addition to the standard inverse distance method, on both spot-based (DLPFC Visium) and an imaging-based (ovary MERFISH) ST datasets (Figs S and T in  S1 Text ). For each combination, we conducted clustering on the spatially smoothed principal components, and computed ARI relative to ground truth annotations, sweeping across a range of kNN and  β  parameters (as well as kernel decay settings for the alternative weightings).  Across both datasets, our results demonstrate that no alternative metric or kernel provided a consistent or significant improvement over inverse Euclidean distance weighting. In all cases, ARI values were highly similar for different distance and kernel choices across the full parameter grid, indicating that the simpler and biologically motivated approach of inverse Euclidean weighting is both effective and robust. These findings justify our default choice of Euclidean distance and inverse distance weighting for RASP, balancing biological plausibility, computational efficiency, and empirical performance.     3 Discussion  Spatially informed dimensionality reduction of ST data is crucial for downstream tasks such as spatial domain identification, cell type annotation, and reduced rank gene signature reconstruction. In this study, we described RASP, a computationally efficient spatially informed dimensionality reduction method that seamlessly integrates into the standard analysis workflow provided by the Scanpy package. RASP utilizes randomized PCA followed by spatial smoothing to generate latent variables that can be leveraged for a wide range of downstream analyses including clustering to predict cell types or spatial domains. RASP also facilitates the reduced rank reconstruction of spatially smoothed gene signatures, enhancing the interpretability of transcriptomic data in spatial contexts. An important feature of RASP is its support for the incorporation of non-transcriptomic covariates via an additional round of randomized PCA. Our findings demonstrate that RASP achieves similar, or higher, accuracy than existing methods for cell type and spatial domain detection tasks, with runtime performance that is orders-of-magnitude faster. RASP can flexibly accommodate various tissue types and ST technologies. Specifically, RASP accurately identifies biologically relevant tissue domains in structures that are homogeneous in size and shape, such as in the DLPFC dataset, while also providing robust labels akin to cell types in the highly heterogeneous mouse ovary sample. Notably, RASP is currently the only method among the techniques we evaluated that can efficiently handle the massive datasets produced by the 10x Xenium platform.   3.1 Parameter selection considerations  Several parameters require careful consideration when applying the RASP method to ST data. These include kNN threshold,  β  value, and the number of PCs to compute. To simplify parameter selection, we provide a recommended range of values for each parameter. Please see  Table 1  for details.  Note that we chose to use inverse distance weighting instead of the more commonly employed Gaussian kernel weighting given the more direct biological interpretation (e.g., inverse squared distances correspond to the concentration of a secreted molecule) and increased flexibility (i.e., users can control both the power parameter and diagonal values instead of just a bandwidth parameter). While RASP defaults to inverse distance weighting, the method can be used with alternative distance metrics and smoothing approaches, each with different characteristics and potential benefits/disadvantages.    3.2 Non-transcriptomic covariates  The RASP method allows for the incorporation of additional location-specific covariates via a two-stage randomized PCA (these are specified using the covariate matrix  Y  in Algorithm 1). Potential covariates include local cell density and cell volume (for technologies that provide this information), the library size of each location/cell, and protein abundance estimates (for technologies that support joint transcriptomic/proteomic measurements). However, it is important to note that using cell density may be somewhat redundant, as the kNN threshold inherently accounts for local density variations. However, depending on the cluster algorithm, this covariate can still impart useful information (see  Fig 3B ). Therefore, users should carefully select these parameters based on the specific objectives of their analysis. RASP’s fast runtime allows users to quickly screen a large range of parameter values to identify the optimal configuration. RASP contains functionality to quickly calculate Moran’s I and CHAOS scores on the resulting clusters and select the appropriate parameters for the final implementation. This is important because it allows users to leverage a priori knowledge to incorporate biologically relevant covariates that are not present in the transcriptomic data in a flexible manner, functionality other tools lack.    3.3 Limitations  While RASP has numerous advantages relative to existing spatially aware dimensionality reduction techniques, it is not without limitations. One of the primary concerns involves the specification of user-provided parameters. Although the default parameters are generally appropriate for a variety of situations, RASP’s smoothing threshold parameter can profoundly influence clustering results. Some degree of trial and error is often necessary to optimize this parameter. However, unlike competing tools that may require upwards of 30 minutes to run, RASP executes quickly, facilitating a straightforward optimization process for users. To assist with parameter selection, we provide guidelines that can help streamline this aspect of the workflow (Table B in  S1 Text ). Additionally, it is important to note that for certain datasets, RASP may not be the best performing method. For instance, in the task of cortical layer assignment in the DLPFC, models such as BASS outperform RASP. Additionally the RASP-based reduced rank gene reconstruction assumes that nearby cells have similar expression levels. However, this is not necessarily the case, and smoothing across tissue boundaries can occur when RASP’s kNN parameter is set at a large value. We recommend that RASP-based reduced rank reconstruction be used primarily for visualization purposes.    3.4 Future directions  Multi-slice alignment and integration of sections from the same organism over different time points are two areas that have witnessed numerous computational innovations over the last five years. Methods such as MOFA, MEFESTO and moscot utilize matrix factorization-based models to simultaneously model both temporal and spatial data [ 60 – 62 ]. PALMO employs variance decomposition analysis and incorporates some spatial modeling capabilities [ 63 ]. In contrast, methods such as PASTE2 and DeST-OT utilize optimal transport principles to align sections from the same tissue sample, enabling 3D models [ 64 , 65 ]. Despite their promising capabilities, these models are computationally intensive, do not scale well to large datasets, and, importantly, lack streamlined approaches for joint dimensionality reduction and clustering. In the current study, we evaluated RASP’s performance on single sections of ST data. Future directions include scaling RASP to support joint spatially informed dimensionality reduction of multiple ST slices, encompassing various tissues or multiple time points. While this enhancement can be simply realized using RASP by analyzing the concatenation of the cell-by-gene and coordinate matrices, how best to handle potential batch effects is a non-trivial problem. Given its computational efficiency, RASP stands out as the sole method capable of jointly reducing massive subcellular ST datasets. Another promising avenue of investigation involves integrating multi-modal information into the spatial reduction process. For instance, data related to protein abundance from methodologies like CITE-seq or chromatin accessibility assessed via spatial ATAC-seq could significantly enhance spatial domain detection [ 66 , 67 ]. RASP already includes functionality to support the incorporation of non-transciptomic covariates, and future research will focus on understanding the impact of these diverse data types in improving spatial domain detection and characterization.     4 Methods   4.1 RASP method  One of the primary motivations for spatially informed dimensionality reduction of ST data is the identification of spatial domains via unsupervised clustering. Clustering on standard PCs is often sufficient to identify cell types, but identification of larger tissue structures benefits from spatial information. The RASP method performs dimensionality reduction and spatial smoothing on normalized ST data and an optional set of location-specific covariates. The two-stage approach used by RASP was chosen to optimize computational efficiency and support the specification of covariates with an overall goal of enabling the flexible and efficient analysis of high-resolution ST datasets. Specifically, RASP uses a sparse matrix representation of the ST data, performs dimensionality reduction using randomized PCA, and generates spatially smoothed PCs using inverse distance weights sparsified according to a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) threshold ( Fig 1A ). To support the integration of location-specific covariates into the latent variables, a second stage randomized PCA is optionally performed on the matrix created by appending the smoothed covariates to the smoothed PCs generated in the first stage. The spatially smoothed PCs generated by the RASP method have utility in a wide range of downstream analyses with clustering and reduced rank reconstruction of gene-level expression important use cases. A detailed description of the method is provided by Algorithm 1. For readability, this version of the algorithm automatically applies the same spatial smoothing to both the first stage PCs and the covariates, however, flexible smoothing of the covariates is supported so that users have control over whether to apply smoothing to each covariate and, if applied, the type of threshold that is employed.

Specifically, clustering was performed by first computing a nearest neighbors distance matrix and a neighborhood graph of spatial locations as described in Mclnnes et al., 2018 [ 68 ]. See Sect 1.1 in  S1 Text  for programming language specific implementation. Note that the distances used for constructing this kNN graph are measured on the spatially smoothed PCs and capture transcriptomic differences between spatial locations, which is distinct from the spatial distances between coordinates used in RASP Algorithm 1. Construction of the neighborhood graph requires specification of the number of nearest neighbors, with the recommended value being between 5 and 50. In general, the number of nearest neighbors should be set based on the size of the target spatial features. For example, users interested in cell type annotation are advised to set the threshold to a smaller value between 5 and 10, while those seeking to annotate spatial domains may consider increasing the threshold above 20. In most cases, a default of 10 is sufficient.  Distinct clusters representing spatial domains or cell types are then computed on the kNN graph using a user-defined clustering algorithm. The RASP method currently supports the use                  M  c  l  u  s  t   ,   L  o  u  v  a  i  n   ,   L  e  i  d  e  n      , and  Walktrap  methods. Note that for large datasets, users may want to avoid the use of the  Walktrap  clustering method as the computational complexity of the algorithm will increase runtime to an unreasonable level on a local machine.    4.3 RASP-based reduced rank reconstruction of gene-level expression  In addition to domain identification, an important application of spatially smoothed PCs is the reconstruction of gene-level expression values. Reduced rank reconstruction is motivated by the fact that the biological signal in transcriptomic data typically has a much lower rank than the rank of the observed measurements. Projecting ST data onto a lower dimensional space borrows the signal from correlated genes and can effectively mitigate both sparsity and noise [ 34 ]. For the spatially smoothed PCs generated by RASP Algorithm 1, the reconstruction process follows Algorithm 2.
